metaDescription: Five solar generators in the 4kW class compared on 240V output, transfer switch readiness, capacity and expandability for real home circuit backup.
expertTake: The EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Classic is the pick for a true 4000W output with a 5kWh starter pack and a long expansion path. The Jackery HomePower 3600 Pro Max is the choice for a clean transfer switch install with a 10ms UPS. Skip the class if you only plan to run a few plug in loads, because a 3kWh station does that for far less.
introParagraphs: Once a solar generator moves past the compact appliance tier, the conversation changes from plugging devices into a box to wiring a box into a house. Stations in this heavy class are the first that can feed a 240 volt circuit, which opens the door to a well pump, an electric dryer or a larger air conditioner without paralleling two units.

Capacity, split phase output, transfer switch compatibility and how the system grows later are what separate good choices here. The inverter number is mostly shared, so the buying decision lives in the fine print about voltage, expansion and the speed of the backup switch.

products.name: EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Classic 5017Wh 4000W

specList.label: Target
specList.value: Fridge, microwave, CPAP, Wi-Fi at once

products.description:
EcoFlow's TITAN 5000 Classic is the only pick here that actually lists a 4,000W rated output, rather than a smaller number paired with a big surge claim. Its 5017Wh LiFePO4 pack gives roughly 4,200Wh of usable AC energy, enough for one day of fridge, microwave, CPAP, Wi-Fi and lighting together. EcoFlow says the platform expands from 5kWh to 30kWh, which is the longest growth path of any unit in this guide.

The drawbacks are weight and price. This is a large cabinet class unit, not something you carry, and it sits at the upper tiers of the guide. It also lacks the bundled panels of the Jackery kits, so you must plan the array separately. Set against the Jackery 3600 Pro Max, you gain nearly 1.4kWh of starting capacity but lose the compact footprint.

Ownership favors planning. Mount it on a level floor with space for airflow, keep it dry and away from a garage door that sees freezing wind, and charge it to about 50 percent if the home sees no storms for months. It is the best pick for a household that wants a durable, expandable backup for the long term. A sensible first setup is the base unit plus a ground mounted array of 800W or more, which gives a meaningful daily solar contribution during a long outage, and the first expansion battery once you have lived with the real nightly draw of your own household.
products.bestFor: Homeowners building a long term expandable backup with a true 4000W output.
pros: Can run fridge, microwave and CPAP together
cons: Very heavy and not truly portable

products.name: Jackery HomePower 3600 Pro Max 3584Wh, 120V and 240V
products.description:
The Pro Max reads the 4000W label differently: its 4000W figure applies at 240V, while 120V circuits get 2000W. That means it is built around a home panel, and Jackery says it can sit behind a manual transfer switch for a 4kW to 8kW backup setup. The 10ms UPS keeps computers and routers up through the swap, which is faster than the 20ms rating on the HomePower 3000.

The price of that design is a lower plug in output. If you plan to run a fridge and a microwave from standard outlets, 2000W per leg is the limit, and a hot appliance like a space heater or a kettle will exceed it. The 3584Wh pack is smaller than EcoFlow's 5017Wh, so a long outage burns through it sooner. The bundled 2x200W panels add about 240 to 320W of real harvest.

In use, a transfer switch install is the correct way to power a home panel, and it should be done by a licensed electrician. Keep the unit indoors, charge to partial level for storage and update firmware via the app. Buy it if you plan on wiring it to the house with Jackery service behind it.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who plan a transfer switch install and need a fast 240V capable backup.
cons: Needs a proper transfer switch for panel backup

products.name: Jackery Solar Generator 5000 Plus 5040Wh 7200W
products.description:
Jackery's 5000 Plus sits above this guide's 4kW label with a 7200W rating and a 14,400W surge, making it the most capable machine in the group. Go here if you want to run an electric dryer, a well pump and a fridge from one box, and the company claims about 13 days of home backup on a full 60kWh stack. The 5040Wh base pack is similar in size to EcoFlow's.

It costs the most, and the extra inverter power is only useful if your loads need it. For a typical fridge and lighting setup, you are paying for capacity you will not use. The bundled 2x200W panels are a small input for a pack this large, so expect four to five days of solar to refill it.

Ownership is about infrastructure: this is a floor standing, heavy unit that wants a dedicated spot and an electrician's help for panel integration. LFP cells and a 10 year life claim support long term use, though the claim is a vendor figure. Keep it dry and ventilated and charge to about half for long storage. It suits those who want a single machine to run most of a home during an outage.
products.bestFor: Larger households wanting a 7200W unit that can stack toward whole home backup.
cons: Panels bundled are small for the pack
More power than most homes need

products.name: SolarPlay Q3600 3840Wh 3600W with 400W panel

specList.label: Charge
specList.value: 0 to 100% in 1.5 hours with AC and 2000W solar

products.description:
SolarPlay's Q3600 holds 3840Wh of LiFePO4 energy and a 3600W inverter with a 5500W surge, at a lower price tier than the Jackery stations. It claims a full charge in about 1.5 hours when AC and a 2000W solar array are used together, which is useful if you can connect a large array. The bundled 400W panel gives 240 to 320W in real conditions.

It falls short of a true 4000W class: the 3600W rating is a 120V figure, with no 240V split phase and no transfer switch focus. For a household that wants plug in backup rather than panel integration, that is fine. For a well pump on 240V, it is the wrong tool. The brand is newer and offers less service detail than Jackery or EcoFlow.

In ownership terms, use it as a heavy plug in power station: keep it indoors, mind the weight and use a heavy gauge extension. Store at around half charge, clear dust from the fan, and avoid using it at full load for hours. On capacity per dollar it leads, provided you do not need 240V. A practical test before you buy is to list every appliance you want running together and add their label watts, because a total above 3,600W will trip the inverter no matter how big the surge rating on the box looks.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want 3.8kWh and a 400W panel at the lowest tier for plug in loads only.
pros: Fast 1.5 hour charge with AC and solar combined
cons: 3600W falls short of a true 4000W class

products.name: ABOK Ark3600 3840Wh with 400W panel, TT-30
products.description:
ABOK's Ark3600 is the mobile pick of this lineup, with a TT-30 outlet for RV shore cords and a 2000W solar input that can charge fast from a big array. Its 3600W rating with a 7200W peak is strong for motor starts, and the 3840Wh LiFePO4 pack gives it the same energy as the SolarPlay with more expansion headroom.

Like the SolarPlay, it is a 120V machine with no 240V output, which makes it a poor match for a home panel without help. The bundled 400W panel is modest for a 3.8kWh pack, so one sunny day recovers only about 1.2 to 1.6kWh. Different listings pair the same station with 200W, 400W or alternator chargers, and they are one machine.

In ownership, secure it in a van or camper with a fixed mount, inspect the TT-30 and solar connectors, and keep it ventilated. LiFePO4 handles heat well, but prolonged hot cab storage is still a bad idea. It answers for owners who move between a house and a vehicle and want one station for both. Check the shore power cord you own before buying, since a 30A TT-30 plug is common on smaller trailers while many larger coaches use 50A, and a station that matches your plug saves buying an adapter and avoids derating the circuit.
products.bestFor: Van and RV owners who also want occasional home outage use.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A true 4000W class unit should offer 240V, since a single 120V leg is limited to about 1,800 to 2,000W by wiring. The Jackery 3600 Pro Max delivers 4000W at 240V but only 2000W at 120V, while the SolarPlay and ABOK are 120V only. If your pump or dryer is 240V, only the Pro Max, 5000 Plus and EcoFlow can serve it.

The EcoFlow TITAN lists 4000W continuous, the Jackery 5000 Plus 7200W, while the SolarPlay's 5500W is surge. A surge number only lasts a moment. Always plan the continuous load of what runs together, then add the largest starting surge.

EcoFlow's 5017Wh and Jackery's 5040Wh give about 4,200Wh usable, while the 3584Wh Pro Max gives about 3,000Wh. At a 1kW average load that is 4.2 versus 3 hours. Larger packs matter more than the inverter for outages lasting a day or more.

Feeding a home panel safely needs a manual transfer switch or an interlock installed by an electrician. Jackery describes the Pro Max with a transfer switch for 4kW to 8kW backup. Never back feed a panel through a dryer outlet, since it energizes the grid and endangers line workers.

EcoFlow lists 30kWh, Jackery 5000 Plus 60kWh and the Pro Max 43kWh, while the ABOK reaches 11.5kWh. An expansion path lets you start small and grow. Confirm that expansion batteries are sold separately and priced reasonably.

A 400W bundled panel gives about 240 to 320W, so a 3.8kWh pack needs 12 to 16 sun hours. Big arrays require matching the controller's voltage and wattage input, such as the ABOK's 2000W. Plan the array separately for long outages.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voltage compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which units supply 240V and at what power. The Pro Max, 5000 Plus and EcoFlow can serve 240V loads, while the SolarPlay and ABOK are 120V only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Usable energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We multiplied each pack's watt-hours by 85 percent. The EcoFlow and Jackery 5000 Plus provide around 4,200Wh, the 3840Wh units about 3,260Wh and the Pro Max about 3,050Wh.

howWeEvaluated.title: Expansion and ecosystem
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the maximum stack each system supports and whether expansion batteries are listed. EcoFlow's 30kWh and Jackery's 43kWh and 60kWh outrank the ABOK's 11.5kWh.

howWeEvaluated.title: Backup behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for UPS claims and transfer switch guidance. The Pro Max's 10ms UPS and manual transfer switch positioning rate highest.

howWeEvaluated.title: Solar and support
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed bundled panels, solar input limits and brand service. The ABOK's 2000W input and SolarPlay's 400W bundle score well on charging, while Jackery and EcoFlow score best on support.

rows: 4000W at 240V and a transfer switch design

cards.label: 120V plug in
cards.text: The SolarPlay Q3600, ABOK Ark3600 and the EcoFlow TITAN's standard outlets suit extension cord use, running a fridge, microwave and electronics. Setup is simple and needs no electrician.

cards.label: 240V panel backup
cards.text: The Pro Max and 5000 Plus feed 240V circuits and can sit behind a transfer switch to power chosen circuits in the panel. Installation requires a licensed electrician and permits in most areas.

howToChoose.note: Plug in households take the EcoFlow or SolarPlay, and panel integrators take a Jackery.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: 240V output, a transfer switch plan and at least 5kWh. A fridge, freezer, furnace blower and lights average 1 to 2kW, so 5kWh gives a few hours of margin.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Jackery 5000 Plus and EcoFlow TITAN 5000 Classic carry over 5kWh. The Pro Max has the 240V path but a 3584Wh starter pack, so budget extra packs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need 240V or a growth path. The Jackery 5000 Plus and EcoFlow TITAN cost more but carry real home loads and expand over years.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your needs are plug in loads. The SolarPlay Q3600 gives 3840Wh and a 400W panel at the lowest tier, trading 240V and support depth.

maintenance.why: Large packs sit idle for months. Keep around 50 to 60 percent and avoid full discharge.
Loose lugs heat under load. A licensed electrician should check torque and insulation.
Dust raises inverter temperature at heavy load.
High current through worn plugs causes heat and voltage drop.
Power a known load for an hour to confirm the unit still delivers expected runtime.

faq.q: Is a 4,000 watt solar generator enough to run a house?
faq.a: It can run essential circuits such as a fridge, freezer, furnace blower, lights and electronics, but not an entire house with central air and an electric range. Use a transfer switch and choose circuits carefully.

faq.q: What is the difference between 120V and 240V output?
faq.a: A 240V output carries twice the power on the same current and runs well pumps, dryers and some air conditioners. Many 3.6kW units are 120V only, which limits each circuit to about 1,800 to 2,000W.

faq.q: Can I back feed my panel through a dryer outlet?
faq.a: No. Back feeding energizes the grid and can injure line workers. Use a manual transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician.
At a 1kW average load, about 4.2 hours after losses. A fridge and freezer alone use 1 to 2.5kWh a day, so 5kWh can cover essentials for about two days.

faq.q: Are expansion batteries worth planning for?
faq.a: Yes. They turn a starter unit into a long outage system, and the Jackery 5000 Plus and EcoFlow TITAN expand to tens of kWh. Confirm future availability and price before committing.

faq.q: How do I size solar panels for it?
faq.a: A 400W array gives about 240 to 320W in real light, so a 5kWh pack needs two days. Add panels up to the controller's wattage and voltage limit and check connector compatibility.
